page.text:
Although the rational order is dense—meaning there are no 'gaps' in the
sense of immediate predecessors or successors—$\mathbb{Q}$ nonetheless
exhibits profound structural incompleteness.

A classic demonstration discovered by the Pythagoreans is the
incommensurability of the diagonal of a unit square: no rational number
satisfies $x^2 = 2$. For if $x = a/b$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, then
$a^2 = 2b^2$ forces $a$ to be even, say $a = 2k$. Substituting gives
$4k^2 = 2b^2$, so $b^2 = 2k^2$, forcing $b$ to be even as well,
contradicting coprimality.

In order-theoretic terms, the subset
$S = \{q \in \mathbb{Q} : q \leq 0 \text{ or } q^2 < 2\}$ is bounded
above (for example, by $2$), but has no least upper bound in
$\mathbb{Q}$. Similarly, Cauchy sequences of rationals like the
truncations of $\sqrt{2}$ fail to converge to a limit in $\mathbb{Q}$.
This defect necessitates the construction of the real continuum
$\mathbb{R}$ via Dedekind cuts or metric completions.
